intro: “Can” is a very common modal verb. We use it to say what we are able to do, to ask for or give permission, and to ask for help. Its form is very simple, but learners often add “to”, “do” or an s that are not there.
objectifs: Make sentences with can and can't for every subject, with no “to” and no “-s”.
Ask questions with Can…? and answer them (Yes, I can / No, I can't).
Talk about your abilities (I can swim) and say how well (well, a little, not at all).
Ask for, give or refuse permission (Can I…? You can't…).

texte: “Can” is a modal verb: it never changes. No s with he, she, it (“she can”, never “she cans”), and the next verb is in the base form, with no “to”: “I can swim”, never “I can to swim”.
Negative: “cannot” (one word in careful writing) or “can't” (short form, the most common). Question: put “can” before the subject, with no “do”: “Can you swim?”
Short answers: “Yes, I can.” / “No, I can't.” Don't repeat the main verb.

lignes: Yes, subject + can. / No, subject + can't.
Yes, she can. / No, she can't.

exemples: My son can read and write.
Ability.
I can't find my keys!
can't = I try but it's not possible.
Can you speak Spanish? — No, I can't.
Question and short answer.

sections.titre: Ability: what you are able to do
texte: “Can” is for skills you learn (swim, drive, read) and for things you are physically able to do. Say “I can swim”, not “I know swim” or “I know to swim”.
To say how well: “very well”, “well”, “a little”, “not very well”, “can't… at all” (= not in any way). Careful: say “well” (adverb), not “good”.
For languages, say “I can speak English” or simply “I speak English”.
exemples: I can swim, but not very well.
How well: not very well.
My grandmother can't use a computer at all.
not at all = zero.
Can you play the piano? — Yes, a little.
a little = not much.
sections.note: In the past, “can” becomes “could” (I could swim when I was five). For other tenses, use “be able to” (lesson 108).

sections.titre: Permission: Can I…? You can / can't
texte: To ask for permission: “Can I…?”. To be more polite, say “Could I…?” (lesson 57), and in formal English “May I…?”.
To give or refuse permission, or talk about a rule: “You can…” (it's allowed), “You can't…” (it's not allowed).
Natural answers: “Yes, of course.”, “Sure.”, “Go ahead.”; to say no politely: “Sorry, you can't.” or “I'm afraid not.”
exemples: Can I open the window? — Yes, of course.
Asking for permission.
You can't park here. It's for buses.
A rule.
You can use my phone.
Giving permission.

texte: “Can you…?” asks someone to do something for you: “Can you help me?”. “Can I…?” can also offer help: “Can I help you?”.
“Can” also says what is possible: “You can buy tickets online.” Here “you” means “people in general”.
exemples: Can you close the door, please?
A request.
Can I help you? — Yes, I'm looking for the station.
An offer (in a shop, in the street).
You can see the sea from my window.
Possibility.

texte: Never add “do”: “Do you can…?” and “I don't can…” are wrong. “Can” makes questions and negatives on its own.

In speech, “can” and “can't” sound similar. The difference is mostly the vowel and the stress (see pronunciation). If you are not sure, listen to the short answer, which is always clear: “Yes, I can” / “No, I can't”.

formule: subject + can / can't + verb (no to) · Can + subject + verb…? · Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
prononciation: In a positive sentence, “can” is weak and quick: “I can swim” = /aɪ kən ˈswɪm/. Stress the main verb.
“can't” is never weak: /kɑːnt/ in British English (like “aunt” with a k), /kænt/ in American English. Stress can't AND the verb: “I CAN'T SWIM”.
In a short answer, “can” is strong: “Yes, I CAN” /kæn/.
In American English, you hardly hear the t in “can't”; listen to the length and strength of the vowel.
“Can I…?” is linked: /kənaɪ/. The question goes up at the end.
erreurs: After a modal, use the base verb with no “to”.
A modal never takes an s.
No “do”: put can before the subject.
She can speak English very good.
She can speak English very well.
After a verb, use the adverb “well”.
Can I to open the window?

dialogue.contexte: In Quebec City, Moussa has an interview for a summer job in a hotel. Mrs Tremblay asks him questions.
lignes: So, Moussa, can you speak English and French?
Yes, I can. And I can speak a little Spanish too.
No, I can't. But I can ride a bike!
can't is strong; ride a bike.
That's OK. Can you work at the weekend?
Yes, I can work on Saturdays and Sundays. Can I ask a question?
Can staff eat at the hotel restaurant?
staff = the people who work there.
Yes, you can have lunch there for free. But you can't use your phone at reception.

mots: move through water using your arms and legs
My sister can drive a bus.
make a car, bus or lorry move
make music with an instrument; do a sport
take something and give it back later
leave your car in a place
in any way (used with a negative)

items: I'm sorry, I ___ come to your party. I'm at work.
You ___ smoke in the hospital. It's not allowed.
You ___ pay by card here. We accept all cards.

exercices.consigne: Write the question with can and the short answer.
items: Can you swim? — Yes, I can.
Can she cook? — No, she can't.
Can they speak French? — Yes, they can.
Can I sit here? — Yes, you can.
Can he play the piano? — No, he can't.
You can't take photos in the museum.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: He don't can cook at all.
Can I to borrow your pen?

exercices.consigne: Write four sentences: two things you can do (with well or a little) and two things you can't do.
items: I can speak French very well and I can speak a little English. I can cook a good ndolé. I can't drive, and I can't play any musical instrument at all.

a_retenir: can + base verb, no “to”, no s, no “do”: She can swim. Can she swim? She can't swim.
Short answers: Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
Ability: I can swim; say how well with well, a little, not at all.
Permission and rules: Can I…? You can / You can't…; more polite: Could I…?
